summary: Southern catalpa is a short-lived deciduous tree native to the southeastern United States. Its large, heart-shaped leaves bear nectar glands, an unusual feature whose output increases when catalpa hawkmoth caterpillars feed on them. The extra nectar attracts ants that help defend the tree, while the caterpillars tolerate and concentrate chemical compounds that deter more generalist plant-eaters. White, purple-and-gold-marked flowers are followed by long, slender capsules filled with winged seeds, which often remain on the tree through winter.

Stinking goosefoot is a small annual whose native range is uncertain, but is thought to centre on Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of southern Europe and North Africa. Its grey-green, mealy foliage has a strong rotten-fish smell associated with trimethylamine. It favours sunny, bare, nitrogen-rich ground, including old fields, roadsides and places enriched by animal dung, and disappears as vegetation closes in. In Britain, its twentieth-century retreat was linked to changing farming practices and the replacement of manure with chemical fertiliser.

Tōtara is a long-lived podocarp tree endemic to New Zealand. It grows slowly into a large tree with a massive trunk, papery purplish-to-golden-brown bark and stiff, needle-like leaves. Its cones develop bright-red, fleshy scales beneath one or two seeds. The hard, straight-grained and rot-resistant wood was central to Māori carving and canoe building: its relatively light, long timbers could be drilled near the edge without splitting, then lashed together with flax rope for large waka.

details.part: red flesh of the berry-like cones

summary: Japanese skimmia is a dense evergreen shrub native across parts of eastern Asia, from Japan and Taiwan to China, Vietnam, the Philippines and the Russian Far East. Its glossy, oil-dotted leaves and fragrant spring flowers suit the shaded forest floor it occupies in much of Japan. Most varieties have male and female flowers on separate plants, though one variety is an exception. Female plants bear rounded drupes, usually red, while one form produces white fruit.

Sweet-brier is a dense, prickly deciduous rose native to most of Europe; its occurrence as a native plant in western Asia is uncertain. Glandular hairs give the foliage a strong apple-like scent, reflected in the name “sweet”, while pink flowers develop into red hips. Outside its native range it has become invasive in parts of southern South America, southeastern Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. In New Zealand pasture, cattle, possums and birds spread its seeds after eating the hips.

Cedronella canariensis is a tall perennial herb endemic to Macaronesia. It grows in laurel forest and other shady places, generally above 500 metres, and can reach about 1.5 metres high. Each stalked leaf is divided into three serrated, lance-shaped leaflets, with the terminal leaflet larger than the pair beside it. Its flowers are arranged in spikes and have two-lipped corollas shaded from purple and lilac to pink. The leaves were historically prepared as infusions in regional folk medicine.

Ceylon cinnamon is a small evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka. Its inner bark is the spice historically known as cinnamon, a name also applied to cassia from another species. In cultivation, peeled inner bark is dried and sold as quills or ground powder, while crushed twigs, leaves and berries are used to make cinnamon oil. Sri Lanka is described as the leading producer, with commercial cultivation also established in the Seychelles, Madagascar and Tanzania.

summary: Stevia is a tender perennial herb native to parts of Brazil and Paraguay. Its leaves contain steviol glycosides, compounds described as far sweeter than sugar, and are widely cultivated for sweetener extracts. Guaraní communities have used the plant for centuries to sweeten yerba mate and as a sweet treat. Wild plants occur from grassland to mountain terrain, but only a small proportion of their seeds germinate; frost prevents outdoor overwintering in colder climates.

details.use: used to sweeten yerba mate and eaten as a sweet treat
details.scope: centuries-old use by Guaraní people in Brazil and Paraguay

summary: Blue mahoe is a fast-growing flowering tree native to Cuba, Jamaica, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, and is Jamaica’s national tree. Its hibiscus-like flowers shift from bright yellow through orange and red to crimson as they mature. The name “blue” comes from blue-green streaks in its polished wood, which can also show purple, olive, grey and black. This durable, naturally glossy timber is used for furniture, carving, turned objects and musical instruments such as the cuatro.

Purple toadflax is a perennial herb endemic to central and southern Italy, including Sicily. Slender upright stems carry narrow grey-green leaves and a long flowering spike, usually of dark violet or purple blooms, from April to October. In its native range it occupies cliffs, scree, woodland edges and uncultivated ground from sea level into high mountains. It is widely grown and has naturalised in several temperate regions, where its persistent flowers attract bees but it may spread on walls and stony waste ground.

Ornithogalum baeticum is a perennial bulb native to the western Mediterranean, centred on the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa. It grows in damp grassland, scrub clearings, rocky slopes and open woodland. Narrow green leaves carry a white lengthwise stripe that fades during flowering. Its loose cluster bears white flowers with a broad green band on the outside of each tepal; this outer marking covers the bloom when it closes at night or in cloudy weather. Deeply grooved, angular seed capsules help distinguish the species.

The small-flowered tongue-orchid is a compact orchid native around the Mediterranean Basin, the Canary Islands and Europe’s Atlantic coast as far as France. Its greyish-pink sepals and petals form a hood above the flower’s column and tongue-like lip. A colony discovered on an eleventh-floor green roof in London in 2021 prompted a proposal that tiny seeds had arrived on winds associated with Saharan dust; that explanation remains under study with botanical and fungal researchers.

Parsnip palm is a large biennial or perennial of the carrot family found naturally on Madeira. Despite its common name, it forms a spreading crown on a woody stem rather than a true palm trunk. The lower stem becomes leafless and scarred, while finely divided leaves and broad clusters of numerous white to purplish flowers grow above. It favours sunny, well-drained places and roadsides, and after introduction to New Zealand became an invasive pest around Wellington.

Sinapidendron frutescens is a flowering member of the mustard family represented by two described subspecies on Madeira. The supplied account treats both subsp. frutescens and subsp. succulentum as endemic to the Madeira archipelago and states that neither is protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

Anise-scented sage is a perennial subshrub native across a broad part of South America, including Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina. Its spreading roots form large patches, while crushed mint-green leaves release an anise scent. Tall flower spikes carry shades of blue that include an uncommon clear blue, blooming from midsummer until frost in cold regions. Cultivation has carried the species around the world, and it has become naturalised in New Zealand and Chile.

Orange rock hair is a filamentous terrestrial green alga that forms tiny bushy tufts on rocks, old walls, concrete, tree bark, rotting wood, moss and wet soil. Carotenoid pigments mask the green of its cells and give colonies their golden-yellow to orange-brown colour. Each tuft consists of upright filaments rising from a reduced layer of prostrate filaments; the upright threads may be unbranched or densely branched but reach only about 1.5 millimetres tall.

Glory bush is a sprawling evergreen flowering shrub native to Brazil. It bears dark-green, hairy leaves marked by strong lengthwise veins and produces clusters of brilliant purple flowers with contrasting black stamens through summer and autumn. The plant spreads by suckers and can be trained against a trellis. It grows best in acidic, well-drained soil, needs a sunny sheltered position outdoors, and requires winter protection where temperatures approach freezing.

Striped Barbados lily is a bulb-forming perennial herb native to southern and eastern Brazil. It usually carries two to four bright-red flowers, each marked by a green keel that runs halfway along the petal-like segments and by bristles at the throat. The plant produces numerous small bulbs, or bulbils, which help it escape cultivation and become naturalised in tropical areas. Plants raised from seed take about two years to grow.

Great Plains flatsedge is a perennial sedge native to North America, widespread across southeastern Canada and the central and northeastern United States, with scattered western populations. It grows in open, sunny places such as prairies, fields, roadsides and farms. Underground rhizomes allow it to spread, while its upright stems are triangular in cross-section. The flowering spikes gather into a dense, roughly spherical cluster and produce small, dark-brown to nearly black, egg-shaped fruits.

Procumbent pigweed is a smooth, mat-forming annual thought to be native to the central and possibly eastern United States. It flowers from summer into autumn and has spread through most temperate parts of North America as well as South America and Eurasia. Its seeds were food for several Native American peoples; Zuni people first ate them raw and later ground them with black cornmeal, shaping the mixture into balls.

details.use: ground with black cornmeal, formed into balls and eaten
details.conditions: ground and mixed with black cornmeal
details.scope: later historical use among Zuni people

summary: African sandalwood is a semi-parasitic plant found in scattered parts of southern, eastern and northwestern Africa, the Canary Islands and the southern Iberian Peninsula. It usually grows sparsely on rocky ground or along dry-forest margins. Its scented wood is harvested for timber and essential oil, and overexploitation continues in parts of its range despite legal protection. In Somaliland, the leaves and tender branches are also used to tan leather.

Common yellow sedge is a member of the Carex flava species complex, native from Iceland, Macaronesia and Europe east through western Asia to the Himalayas, with possible native occurrence in Greenland. It has also been introduced to eastern Canada, New Jersey and Tasmania. Two subspecies are accepted in the supplied account: subsp. cedercreutzii in the Azores and the more widely distributed subsp. demissa.

reviewFlags: The supplied material provides only the species identity and family, with no narrative evidence for an entry.

summary: Natal bottlebrush is a flowering tree native to South Africa, Eswatini and Lesotho. It grows as a small to medium-sized tree, reaching about 10 metres, with elliptical leaves and distinctive flower clusters shaped like bottlebrushes.

Field fluffweed is a flowering plant in the daisy family. Its native range stretches from Europe through western Siberia to the western Himalayas, with additional native occurrences in the Canary Islands and Morocco.
